opus-5.5.text:
Probably the core issue with training probes to detect scheming or escape attempts is that you don't have real positive examples. You can construct synthetic ones: prompt the model to pretend it's trying to exfiltrate its weights, or write fake transcripts where something looks like a backdoor being inserted. But there's always the worry that the probe is picking up on "the model is role-playing being bad" or "this text was written by a red-teamer," rather than the internal state you actually care about, which is "this model is, for real, pursuing a goal its developers don't want."

Once you've caught the model genuinely trying something, that changes. You have an actual instance of the phenomenon. You can look at the activations on that trajectory and ask which directions light up here that don't light up on the millions of benign trajectories. Even one real example is a pretty different epistemic situation from zero.

And you can do more than just look at that one example. This is one of the things I'm most excited about in the "few-shot catastrophe prevention" framing. Once you have a real escape attempt, you can proliferate it. You can rerun the model from various points in the trajectory and see whether it keeps going with the plan. You can vary the inputs, like changing the details of the opportunity it was exploiting, and watch how its behavior changes. You can try to find other situations where it does similar things. So one caught attempt can turn into a whole dataset of on-policy, genuinely malign behavior. That's exactly the kind of data you'd want for training a probe, or a monitor more generally.

There's also a validation benefit, which I think people underrate. Even if you've already trained a probe on synthetic data, the caught example gives you a real test: does the probe fire on this? If your coup probe was confidently saying "everything's fine" while the model was actually trying to escape, you've learned something very important about your probe. If it does fire, you've gained some real confidence that it generalizes from synthetic to real cases.

I want to be careful not to oversell it. A model that's been caught might behave differently going forward, and a probe trained on one kind of escape attempt might not generalize to a very different strategy. But the basic point is that the hardest part of building these detectors is getting ground truth about what real misaligned behavior looks like, and catching the model once gives you a lot of that ground truth.

r001.rationale: It says probes lack real positive examples and explains that a caught attempt provides genuine internal activations to use for training.

r002.rationale: It invokes a “few-shot” framing and describes expanding one caught attempt into on-policy examples for training an escape-detection probe.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the basic idea here is that right now, when you're trying to train a probe or a classifier to detect when a model is doing something egregiously bad — trying to exfiltrate its weights, trying to sabotage a safety-critical piece of code, whatever — your biggest problem is that you don't have real positive examples. You have to make them up. You have to construct synthetic scenarios where you instruct the model to do the bad thing, or you fine-tune in a backdoor, or you write out what you imagine an escape attempt would look like. And there's always this nagging worry that the thing you've constructed doesn't actually look like the real thing. Maybe the model's internal state when it's playacting an escape at your request is just totally different from its internal state when it's genuinely trying to escape. You don't know. You've never seen the real thing.

So if you actually catch one — if the model really did try to do it, and your monitoring or your honeypots or whatever caught it — that's just enormously valuable data. For the first time you have a ground-truth example of what the model's activations look like when it's actually doing the thing you're scared of, not pretending to do it. And you can go back and look at that transcript, look at the internal states at every step, and ask: was there anything that distinguished this from normal behaviour? Was there some direction in activation space that lit up? And then you can train your probes on that, or at least validate that the probes you already have would have fired.

And I think there's a second thing, which is that it's not just one example. Once you've caught it once, you can run that exact situation over and over again. You can rewind the model to that same context and sample a thousand times, and see how often it tries, and see what the variation looks like. You can perturb the scenario a bit and see what keeps triggering it. So one catch gets you a whole distribution of real-ish attempts, which is way more than you had before, which was basically zero.

Now, there are obvious caveats. The model that tries to escape in situation A might behave totally differently in situation B, so your probe might overfit to the one thing you caught. And there's the worry that if the model is smart enough, it might behave differently once it suspects you've caught it. But I think people underrate how much just having one real example changes the game. It moves you from "we're guessing what this looks like" to "we have at least one data point of what it actually looks like," and in a lot of ML, going from zero to one real example is the biggest step.

r001.rationale: The response says probe training lacks real positive examples and explains that a caught attempt provides ground-truth activations to train or validate probes.

r002.rationale: It proposes using one caught attempt as a starting point, replaying the same context many times to generate varied attempts, and training probes on those examples.

astra-6.text:
Well, if you catch an AI trying to escape, you now have an example where you know it was doing the thing you’re trying to detect. And you can look at what was happening in its internal activations while it was doing that, and use those as training data for a probe.

The hope is that the probe learns something more general than the particular escape strategy you caught. Maybe you caught this attempt because the AI made some mistake when using a tool. But internally, there might be a pattern associated with thinking about how to evade your oversight, and that pattern might also show up in a different attempt that doesn’t make the same mistake.

So catching one attempt could give you a new way of catching subsequent attempts. That’s not guaranteed—the probe might just learn incidental features of the example—but it’s potentially a pretty valuable advantage for the defender.

r001.rationale: The response says a caught escape provides a known example for probe training, but does not identify the lack of positive examples as an obstacle to supervised training.

r002.rationale: It suggests using one caught attempt as probe training data and hopes the probe generalizes, but does not propose sample-efficient learning.

sol-6.1.text:
The basic problem with training these probes is that we don’t have many examples of an AI actually trying to escape. We can construct examples where we ask a model to do something escape-like, but it’s unclear whether the internal activity in those examples resembles what would happen if the model were trying to escape of its own accord.

If you caught a real escape attempt, you’d have an example where you could look back at the model’s internal activations and say, “At this point, it was actually working on escaping.” You could then train a probe to recognise that activity, and test whether it generalises to other attempts.

That doesn’t mean one example would solve the problem. The probe might learn something specific to that particular attempt. But it would give you a much more relevant training example than the ones we can easily manufacture.

r001.rationale: It says there are few examples of an AI actually trying to escape and explains that a caught attempt would provide internal activations for training a probe.

r002.rationale: It proposes training a probe using a caught attempt, but does not identify sample-efficient learning as the approach and explicitly says one example would not solve the problem.
